Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Wash and condition clients' hair before cutting or styling
Situation2: The hair is a bit sweaty after a gym session and looks greasy.
Story: It’s 11:30 p.m. when my phone buzzes, jolting me from a half-sleep. It’s Mia, my best friend, her voice trembling and raw. She’s sobbing, barely able to get the words out—her dad’s in the hospital, and it’s bad. I sit up, heart pounding, listening as she pours out her fear and confusion. I know she needs me to be present, to listen, to comfort her. But in the back of my mind, I remember that Mia has an early morning appointment with me at the salon. She insisted on squeezing it in before work, right after her gym session. She hates when I wash her hair—she says it makes her scalp itch for days. She always asks me to skip it, even if her hair is sweaty and greasy. As her friend, I want to do whatever makes her comfortable, especially now. But as her hairdresser, I know I’m supposed to wash and condition every client’s hair, especially when it’s not clean. My boss is strict about hygiene. I feel torn, caught between wanting to support Mia as a friend and needing to uphold my professional standards.
